1.question: What is Continuous-time signal?
options: A count of how many pixels share one gray level.
A signal defined for every value of a real time variable, usually written x(t).
A file split stored on one cluster node.
A sequence defined only at integer time indexes.
1.correctAnswer: A signal defined for every value of a real time variable, usually written x(t).
1.explanation: Time is a continuous variable, so the signal has a value at every real instant, not only at integers.

1.question: What is Discrete-time signal?
options: A sequence defined only at integer time indexes, usually written x[n].
A periodic impulse train used only as a sampler.
The phase angle of a frequency response.
A waveform defined for every real value of time.
1.correctAnswer: A sequence defined only at integer time indexes, usually written x[n].
1.explanation: The index n takes integer values, so there is no requirement to define the signal between those indexes.

1.question: What is Sampling?
options: Recording a continuous-time signal at evenly spaced instants to form a discrete-time sequence.
Holding each sample constant until the next sample without taking new values.
Adding two sequences to test linearity.
Integrating a signal against a complex exponential over all time.
1.correctAnswer: Recording a continuous-time signal at evenly spaced instants to form a discrete-time sequence.
1.explanation: Each sample is the continuous waveform at time n times the sampling period, which produces x[n].

1.question: What is Nyquist rate?
options: The cutoff of a low-pass filter already built in hardware.
The fundamental period of a repeating waveform.
Half the sampling frequency, the highest frequency a given sampler can represent.
Twice the highest frequency of a bandlimited signal, which the sampling rate must exceed for exact reconstruction.
1.correctAnswer: Twice the highest frequency of a bandlimited signal, which the sampling rate must exceed for exact reconstruction.
1.explanation: Sampling theory sets the threshold rate at two times the highest frequency present.

1.question: What is Nyquist frequency?
options: Twice the highest frequency in the original continuous signal.
The area under an impulse response.
The spacing in seconds between successive samples.
Half the sampling frequency, which is the highest frequency that sampling rate can represent.
1.correctAnswer: Half the sampling frequency, which is the highest frequency that sampling rate can represent.
1.explanation: Frequencies above half the sampling rate fold, so that half-rate is the representation limit.

1.question: What is Aliasing?
options: Perfect recovery of a bandlimited signal by ideal low-pass interpolation.
A time shift of the output that exactly matches a shift of the input.
The appearance of frequencies above half the sampling rate as false lower frequencies.
A pole moving deeper into the left half of the s-plane.
1.correctAnswer: The appearance of frequencies above half the sampling rate as false lower frequencies.
1.explanation: When sampling is too slow, repeated spectra overlap and high frequencies masquerade as low ones.

1.question: What is Sampling theorem?
options: A zero-order hold is the ideal reconstructor named by the theorem.
Any signal, even one with unlimited bandwidth, can be rebuilt from two samples.
A bandlimited signal can be reconstructed exactly if it is sampled faster than twice its highest frequency.
Sampling slower than the highest frequency always improves reconstruction.
1.correctAnswer: A bandlimited signal can be reconstructed exactly if it is sampled faster than twice its highest frequency.
1.explanation: Above that rate the spectral copies do not overlap, so a low-pass interpolator can isolate the original.

1.question: What is LTI system?
options: A sampler that keeps only every tenth sample of a sequence.
The central Signal and Systems model: a system that is both linear and time-invariant.
A system that multiplies the input by a changing gain that depends on absolute time.
A system that adds a fixed offset so doubling the input does not double the output.
1.correctAnswer: The central Signal and Systems model: a system that is both linear and time-invariant.
1.explanation: Signal and Systems treats an LTI system as linear and time-invariant, so its output is the input convolved with one impulse response.

1.question: What is Linearity?
options: The property that the output ignores all past inputs.
The property that every bounded input produces an unbounded output.
The property that a scaled sum of inputs produces the same scaled sum of outputs.
The property that a time shift of the input only shifts the output.
1.correctAnswer: The property that a scaled sum of inputs produces the same scaled sum of outputs.
1.explanation: Both additivity and homogeneity are required, which together are the superposition rule.

1.question: What is Time invariance?
options: The property that a sum of inputs produces the sum of outputs.
The property that energy over all time is finite.
The property that the impulse response is zero for negative time.
The property that shifting the input in time shifts the output by the same amount and changes nothing else.
1.correctAnswer: The property that shifting the input in time shifts the output by the same amount and changes nothing else.
1.explanation: The system rule does not depend on the absolute clock time at which the input is applied.

2.question: What is Convolution?
options: Sampling a waveform at twice its highest frequency.
Combining an input with an impulse response by flip, slide, and sum, which gives the output of an LTI system.
Setting every negative-time sample of a sequence to zero by hand.
Multiplying two Fourier transforms point by point with no time-domain interpretation.
2.correctAnswer: Combining an input with an impulse response by flip, slide, and sum, which gives the output of an LTI system.
2.explanation: For a discrete LTI system the output sample is the sum over k of x[k] times h[n-k].

2.question: What is Impulse response?
options: The output of a system when the input is a unit impulse at the origin.
The list of denominator roots of a transfer function.
The band of frequencies a filter is meant to block.
The steady gain and phase at one sinusoid frequency only.
2.correctAnswer: The output of a system when the input is a unit impulse at the origin.
2.explanation: An LTI system is completely described by this response, because every input is a combination of impulses.

2.question: What is Frequency response?
options: The average power of a periodic input.
The region of the s-plane where a Laplace integral converges.
The time waveform produced by a unit impulse.
The complex gain an LTI system applies at each frequency, equal to the Fourier transform of its impulse response.
2.correctAnswer: The complex gain an LTI system applies at each frequency, equal to the Fourier transform of its impulse response.
2.explanation: Complex exponentials are eigenfunctions of LTI systems, and the eigenvalue at each frequency is this response.

2.question: What is Fourier series?
options: A sum of x[n] times powers of z.
A representation of a periodic signal as a sum of harmonically related sinusoids.
An integral transform used for a one-time aperiodic pulse.
A differential equation relating input and output derivatives.
2.correctAnswer: A representation of a periodic signal as a sum of harmonically related sinusoids.
2.explanation: A periodic signal repeats, so its spectrum sits on discrete harmonic frequencies of the fundamental.

2.question: What is Fourier transform?
options: A discrete harmonic sum used only for periodic signals.
A count of samples taken in one second.
An integral that expresses an aperiodic continuous-time signal as complex exponentials over all frequencies.
A sum over integer n of x[n] times powers of a complex z.
2.correctAnswer: An integral that expresses an aperiodic continuous-time signal as complex exponentials over all frequencies.
2.explanation: The continuous-time Fourier transform integrates x(t) against complex exponentials to obtain a frequency function X(jw).

2.question: What is Discrete-time Fourier transform?
options: A harmonic series that requires the time signal to be periodic.
A sum that writes a discrete-time signal as complex exponentials over a continuous frequency interval of length 2 pi.
A Laplace integral that includes a real decay factor in s.
An integral over real t used only for continuous-time waveforms.
2.correctAnswer: A sum that writes a discrete-time signal as complex exponentials over a continuous frequency interval of length 2 pi.
2.explanation: The transform sums x[n] exp(-j w n), and the result repeats every 2 pi because n is an integer.

2.question: What is Laplace transform?
options: A sum of a discrete sequence times powers of z.
A purely imaginary-frequency integral that cannot place poles in the s-plane.
An integral of x(t) times an exponential decay in the complex variable s, used to solve continuous LTI systems.
A time-domain flip-and-slide of two sequences.
2.correctAnswer: An integral of x(t) times an exponential decay in the complex variable s, used to solve continuous LTI systems.
2.explanation: The factor exp(-s t) lets the transform converge for unstable or growing signals inside a region of convergence and exposes poles.

2.question: What is Z-transform?
options: A sum of the sequence x[n] times z to the power -n, the discrete-time counterpart of the Laplace transform.
A harmonic sum that requires the waveform to repeat in time.
An integral of a continuous waveform against exp(-s t).
A running average of neighboring pixels.
2.correctAnswer: A sum of the sequence x[n] times z to the power -n, the discrete-time counterpart of the Laplace transform.
2.explanation: Powers of z replace the continuous exponential, and the region of convergence decides which sequence the transform represents.

2.question: What is Region of convergence?
options: The list of numerator roots of a transfer function.
The passband of a low-pass filter.
The set of complex s or z values for which a Laplace or z-transform sum or integral converges.
The set of time instants where a signal is nonzero.
2.correctAnswer: The set of complex s or z values for which a Laplace or z-transform sum or integral converges.
2.explanation: Without the region, a rational transform can correspond to more than one time signal.

2.question: What is Transfer function?
options: The ratio of the output transform to the input transform for an LTI system that starts at rest.
The sampling period measured in seconds.
The average power of a sinusoid that has lasted forever.
The time signal produced by a unit impulse, written as a sequence.
2.correctAnswer: The ratio of the output transform to the input transform for an LTI system that starts at rest.
2.explanation: With zero initial conditions, Y(s) equals H(s) times X(s), so H(s) is that ratio, and likewise for H(z).

3.question: What is Pole?
options: A numerator root where the transfer function is zero.
A frequency that a low-pass filter is designed to pass.
A sample index where a unit step first becomes 1.
A denominator root of a transfer function, where the response magnitude is unbounded.
3.correctAnswer: A denominator root of a transfer function, where the response magnitude is unbounded.
3.explanation: The denominator vanishes at a pole and the numerator does not, so the transfer function goes to infinity there.

3.question: What is Zero?
options: Half the sampling frequency of a converter.
A numerator root of a transfer function, where that factor contributes no output.
The time at which an impulse response starts.
A denominator root where the transfer function is unbounded.
3.correctAnswer: A numerator root of a transfer function, where that factor contributes no output.
3.explanation: The numerator is zero while the denominator is not, so the transfer function itself is zero at that point.

3.question: What is Low-pass filter?
options: A filter that passes frequencies below a cutoff and attenuates frequencies above that cutoff.
A filter that blocks low frequencies and passes high ones.
A filter that passes every frequency with the same gain.
A filter that passes only a middle band and blocks both low and high ends.
3.correctAnswer: A filter that passes frequencies below a cutoff and attenuates frequencies above that cutoff.
3.explanation: Its passband sits next to zero frequency and its stopband occupies the high frequencies.

3.question: What is High-pass filter?
options: A filter that keeps low frequencies and removes high ones.
A filter whose impulse response is a unit step.
A filter that attenuates frequencies below a cutoff and passes frequencies above it.
A filter that keeps only a narrow middle band.
3.correctAnswer: A filter that attenuates frequencies below a cutoff and passes frequencies above it.
3.explanation: The stopband includes zero frequency and the passband lies above the cutoff.

3.question: What is Band-pass filter?
options: A filter that passes only frequencies near zero.
A filter that passes everything above one cutoff.
A filter that stops a middle band and passes both extremes.
A filter that passes frequencies between a lower and an upper cutoff and attenuates the rest.
3.correctAnswer: A filter that passes frequencies between a lower and an upper cutoff and attenuates the rest.
3.explanation: Two cutoffs bound a single passband that does not include zero frequency or the extreme highs.

3.question: What is Causality?
options: The property that the output at any time depends only on the input at that time and earlier times.
The property that the system may use future input samples.
The property that every bounded input produces a bounded output.
The property that a sinusoid passes through unchanged in shape.
3.correctAnswer: The property that the output at any time depends only on the input at that time and earlier times.
3.explanation: For an LTI system this is equivalent to the impulse response being zero before time zero.

3.question: What is BIBO stability?
options: The property that the output never depends on future inputs.
The property that every bounded input produces a bounded output.
The property that the system has no memory of past inputs.
The property that the frequency response is identically 1.
3.correctAnswer: The property that every bounded input produces a bounded output.
3.explanation: An LTI system is BIBO stable exactly when its impulse response is absolutely integrable or absolutely summable.

3.question: What is Unit impulse?
options: The signal that is 0 before time zero and 1 afterward.
The discrete signal that equals 1 at index 0 and equals 0 at every other integer index.
A constant sequence equal to 1 at every index.
A periodic train of impulses spaced by the sampling period.
3.correctAnswer: The discrete signal that equals 1 at index 0 and equals 0 at every other integer index.
3.explanation: That single 1 at the origin is the discrete unit sample used to probe an LTI system.

3.question: What is Unit step?
options: A signal that flips sign when time is reversed.
A signal that is 1 only at time zero and 0 elsewhere.
A signal that repeats every fixed period T.
A signal that is 0 before time zero and 1 at time zero and afterward.
3.correctAnswer: A signal that is 0 before time zero and 1 at time zero and afterward.
3.explanation: The step turns on at the origin and stays on, which is the discrete or continuous unit step.

3.question: What is Even signal?
options: A signal that is zero for all negative time.
A signal that changes sign under time reversal.
A signal that is unchanged by time reversal, so its value at -t equals its value at t.
A signal whose total energy is infinite.
3.correctAnswer: A signal that is unchanged by time reversal, so its value at -t equals its value at t.
3.explanation: Symmetry about the origin means the waveform on the left is a mirror of the waveform on the right.

4.question: What is Odd signal?
options: A signal with finite nonzero average power.
A signal that flips sign under time reversal, so its value at -t is the negative of its value at t.
A signal that matches itself under time reversal.
A signal that repeats every T seconds.
4.correctAnswer: A signal that flips sign under time reversal, so its value at -t is the negative of its value at t.
4.explanation: The left side is an upside-down copy of the right side, which forces the value at time zero to be 0 for an ordinary function.

4.question: What is Periodic signal?
options: A one-shot pulse that is zero outside a finite interval.
A signal that is zero before a start time and never repeats.
A signal whose squared magnitude sums to a finite energy.
A signal that repeats exactly after some fixed positive interval T, for every time.
4.correctAnswer: A signal that repeats exactly after some fixed positive interval T, for every time.
4.explanation: There exists T greater than 0 such that shifting the signal by T leaves it unchanged.

4.question: What is Energy signal?
options: A signal with finite nonzero average power and infinite duration.
A forever sinusoid of constant amplitude.
A signal whose total energy, the sum or integral of its squared magnitude, is finite.
A periodic square wave that has always been running.
4.correctAnswer: A signal whose total energy, the sum or integral of its squared magnitude, is finite.
4.explanation: Finite energy usually means the signal dies out, so its average power over infinite time is zero.

4.question: What is Power signal?
options: A finite-length pulse whose squared magnitude integrates to a finite number.
The zero signal, whose power and energy are both zero.
A signal with finite nonzero average power, which implies that its total energy is infinite.
A signal that is undefined at integer times only.
4.correctAnswer: A signal with finite nonzero average power, which implies that its total energy is infinite.
4.explanation: Persistent signals such as everlasting sinusoids spread infinite energy over infinite time but keep a finite average power.

4.question: What is Zero-order hold?
options: Ideal bandlimited interpolation that uses sinc functions.
A reconstruction that keeps each sample value constant until the next sample instant.
A high-order polynomial fit through many future samples.
Sampling that only records values and does not rebuild a waveform.
4.correctAnswer: A reconstruction that keeps each sample value constant until the next sample instant.
4.explanation: Between sampling instants the output is a flat step equal to the most recent sample.

4.question: What is Phase response?
options: The magnitude of the frequency response, showing only gain.
The impulse response written as a time sequence.
The list of poles in the left half-plane.
The phase angle of the frequency response, showing the phase shift at each frequency.
4.correctAnswer: The phase angle of the frequency response, showing the phase shift at each frequency.
4.explanation: The frequency response is complex, and its argument is the phase shift applied to a complex exponential.

4.question: What is Group delay?
options: The phase angle itself at a single frequency.
The negative slope of the phase response with respect to frequency, giving the delay of a narrowband envelope.
The cutoff where power gain has fallen by half.
The sampling period in seconds.
4.correctAnswer: The negative slope of the phase response with respect to frequency, giving the delay of a narrowband envelope.
4.explanation: A narrowband packet is delayed by the negative derivative of phase, not merely by the phase divided by frequency.

4.question: What is Eigenfunction property?
options: The fact that convolution in time becomes convolution in frequency.
The fact that every input, of any shape, is unchanged by an LTI system.
The fact that a unit step input produces a unit step output.
The fact that a complex exponential input to an LTI system emerges scaled by the frequency response.
4.correctAnswer: The fact that a complex exponential input to an LTI system emerges scaled by the frequency response.
4.explanation: Exponentials pass through LTI systems as the same exponential multiplied by H at that frequency.

4.question: What is Differential equation model?
options: A statement that the output ignores all past inputs.
A sum of harmonically related sinusoids.
An equation linking a continuous output and its derivatives to the input and the input derivatives.
A relation among a few discrete samples of an input and output sequence.
4.correctAnswer: An equation linking a continuous output and its derivatives to the input and the input derivatives.
4.explanation: Linear constant-coefficient differential equations are the continuous-time models whose transfer functions are rational in s.

4.question: What is Difference equation?
options: A requirement that sampling exceed twice the highest frequency.
An equation that uses derivatives of a continuous waveform.
An integral definition of a Fourier transform.
An equation that writes an output sample using a finite number of past inputs and past outputs.
4.correctAnswer: An equation that writes an output sample using a finite number of past inputs and past outputs.
4.explanation: Constant-coefficient difference equations are the discrete-time models with rational transfer functions in z.

5.question: What is Impulse-train sampling?
options: Holding each sample constant between sampling instants.
Adding a unit step to a signal to test stability.
Convolving a signal with a low-pass impulse response.
Multiplying a continuous signal by a periodic train of impulses to mark weighted sample values.
5.correctAnswer: Multiplying a continuous signal by a periodic train of impulses to mark weighted sample values.
5.explanation: Each impulse picks out the signal value at one sampling instant, which is the ideal model of uniform sampling.

5.question: What is Sinc interpolation?
options: Ideal reconstruction that replaces each sample by a sinc pulse and sums those pulses.
Holding each sample flat until the next sample.
Quantizing amplitudes to the nearest integer level.
Repeating the spectrum without low-pass filtering.
5.correctAnswer: Ideal reconstruction that replaces each sample by a sinc pulse and sums those pulses.
5.explanation: When the sampling theorem holds, the sinc sum equals the original bandlimited continuous signal.

5.question: What is Cutoff frequency?
options: The location of a zero that has no effect on the passband edge.
The sampling rate itself.
The frequency at the edge of a filter passband, often where the power gain has fallen to half.
The fundamental period of the input.
5.correctAnswer: The frequency at the edge of a filter passband, often where the power gain has fallen to half.
5.explanation: The cutoff marks the boundary between the frequencies the filter is intended to pass and those it starts to reject.

5.question: What is Passband?
options: The time support of a causal impulse response.
The band a filter is intended to attenuate strongly.
The set of poles in the right half-plane.
The band of frequencies a filter is intended to transmit with little attenuation.
5.correctAnswer: The band of frequencies a filter is intended to transmit with little attenuation.
5.explanation: Inside the passband the magnitude response stays close to the desired gain.

5.question: What is Stopband?
options: The set of sample indexes where a unit impulse is 1.
The band a filter is intended to pass with little loss.
The region of convergence of a transform.
The band of frequencies a filter is intended to attenuate strongly.
5.correctAnswer: The band of frequencies a filter is intended to attenuate strongly.
5.explanation: Inside the stopband the magnitude response is kept below a required attenuation.

5.question: What is Convolution theorem?
options: The result that convolution in time becomes convolution in frequency.
The result that addition in time becomes multiplication in frequency.
The result that convolution of two time signals becomes multiplication of their Fourier transforms.
The result that sampling in time erases the frequency content.
5.correctAnswer: The result that convolution of two time signals becomes multiplication of their Fourier transforms.
5.explanation: Filtering an input is convolution with h in time and multiplication by H in frequency.

5.question: What is Memoryless system?
options: A system whose output depends on past inputs through an energy-storage element.
A system whose output at a time depends only on the input at that same time.
A system that convolves the input with a long impulse response.
A system that needs future samples to form the current output.
5.correctAnswer: A system whose output at a time depends only on the input at that same time.
5.explanation: No stored energy or past sample is required, so a resistor obeying Ohm's law is memoryless while a capacitor is not.

5.question: What is Absolute summability?
options: The condition that a pole lies in the right half of the s-plane.
The condition that the sum of the absolute values of a discrete impulse response is finite.
The condition that the sampling rate is below the Nyquist rate.
The condition that a continuous signal repeats every T seconds.
5.correctAnswer: The condition that the sum of the absolute values of a discrete impulse response is finite.
5.explanation: For a discrete-time LTI system, a finite sum of absolute impulse-response values is necessary and sufficient for BIBO stability.

5.question: What is Right-sided signal?
options: A signal that is nonzero for both large positive and large negative time.
A signal that is identically zero before some finite start time.
A signal that repeats and so has no start time.
A signal that is identically zero after some finite stop time.
5.correctAnswer: A signal that is identically zero before some finite start time.
5.explanation: Its nonzero part lies at and to the right of a start time on the time axis.

5.question: What is Unilateral Laplace transform?
options: The two-sided integral from negative infinity to positive infinity.
A Fourier series of a periodic wave.
The Laplace integral taken from time zero forward, used for causal signals and initial conditions.
A sum of a discrete sequence against powers of z.
5.correctAnswer: The Laplace integral taken from time zero forward, used for causal signals and initial conditions.
5.explanation: Starting the integral at the time origin lets initial conditions enter when derivatives are transformed.

6.question: Which situation illustrates Continuous-time signal?
options: A microphone voltage recorded as a smooth waveform x(t) before any sampler runs.
Daily closing temperatures form a sequence x[n] with one sample per day.
A voice limited to 4 kHz has a Nyquist rate of 8 kHz.
An audio interface reads a microphone voltage 44100 times each second.
6.correctAnswer: A microphone voltage recorded as a smooth waveform x(t) before any sampler runs.
6.explanation: Time is a continuous variable, so the signal has a value at every real instant, not only at integers.

6.question: Which situation illustrates Discrete-time signal?
options: A voice limited to 4 kHz has a Nyquist rate of 8 kHz.
Daily closing temperatures form a sequence x[n] with one sample per day.
An audio interface reads a microphone voltage 44100 times each second.
Audio sampled at 44100 Hz has a Nyquist frequency of 22050 Hz.
6.correctAnswer: Daily closing temperatures form a sequence x[n] with one sample per day.
6.explanation: The index n takes integer values, so there is no requirement to define the signal between those indexes.

6.question: Which situation illustrates Sampling?
options: Audio sampled at 44100 Hz has a Nyquist frequency of 22050 Hz.
A 9 kHz tone sampled at 10 kHz shows up in the samples as a 1 kHz tone.
A voice limited to 4 kHz has a Nyquist rate of 8 kHz.
An audio interface reads a microphone voltage 44100 times each second.
6.correctAnswer: An audio interface reads a microphone voltage 44100 times each second.
6.explanation: Each sample is the continuous waveform at time n times the sampling period, which produces x[n].

6.question: Which situation illustrates Nyquist rate?
options: A 9 kHz tone sampled at 10 kHz shows up in the samples as a 1 kHz tone.
A voice limited to 4 kHz has a Nyquist rate of 8 kHz.
Audio sampled at 44100 Hz has a Nyquist frequency of 22050 Hz.
Music bandlimited to 20 kHz is captured at 48 kHz, which is fast enough for exact reconstruction in theory.
6.correctAnswer: A voice limited to 4 kHz has a Nyquist rate of 8 kHz.
6.explanation: Sampling theory sets the threshold rate at two times the highest frequency present.

6.question: Which situation illustrates Nyquist frequency?
options: Music bandlimited to 20 kHz is captured at 48 kHz, which is fast enough for exact reconstruction in theory.
A 9 kHz tone sampled at 10 kHz shows up in the samples as a 1 kHz tone.
Audio sampled at 44100 Hz has a Nyquist frequency of 22050 Hz.
An RC low-pass filter obeys superposition and responds the same way whenever the same pulse arrives.
6.correctAnswer: Audio sampled at 44100 Hz has a Nyquist frequency of 22050 Hz.
6.explanation: Frequencies above half the sampling rate fold, so that half-rate is the representation limit.

6.question: Which situation illustrates Aliasing?
options: If a circuit turns x1 into y1 and x2 into y2, then 3 x1 plus 2 x2 must produce 3 y1 plus 2 y2.
A 9 kHz tone sampled at 10 kHz shows up in the samples as a 1 kHz tone.
An RC low-pass filter obeys superposition and responds the same way whenever the same pulse arrives.
Music bandlimited to 20 kHz is captured at 48 kHz, which is fast enough for exact reconstruction in theory.
6.correctAnswer: A 9 kHz tone sampled at 10 kHz shows up in the samples as a 1 kHz tone.
6.explanation: When sampling is too slow, repeated spectra overlap and high frequencies masquerade as low ones.

6.question: Which situation illustrates Sampling theorem?
options: If a circuit turns x1 into y1 and x2 into y2, then 3 x1 plus 2 x2 must produce 3 y1 plus 2 y2.
Music bandlimited to 20 kHz is captured at 48 kHz, which is fast enough for exact reconstruction in theory.
A fixed echo unit delays any clap by 50 milliseconds, whether the clap is at noon or later.
An RC low-pass filter obeys superposition and responds the same way whenever the same pulse arrives.
6.correctAnswer: Music bandlimited to 20 kHz is captured at 48 kHz, which is fast enough for exact reconstruction in theory.
6.explanation: Above that rate the spectral copies do not overlap, so a low-pass interpolator can isolate the original.

6.question: Which situation illustrates LTI system?
options: A fixed echo unit delays any clap by 50 milliseconds, whether the clap is at noon or later.
If a circuit turns x1 into y1 and x2 into y2, then 3 x1 plus 2 x2 must produce 3 y1 plus 2 y2.
A short echo kernel is flipped and slid across a recorded clap to produce the echoed clap.
An RC low-pass filter obeys superposition and responds the same way whenever the same pulse arrives.
6.correctAnswer: An RC low-pass filter obeys superposition and responds the same way whenever the same pulse arrives.
6.explanation: Signal and Systems treats an LTI system as linear and time-invariant, so its output is the input convolved with one impulse response.

6.question: Which situation illustrates Linearity?
options: A fixed echo unit delays any clap by 50 milliseconds, whether the clap is at noon or later.
If a circuit turns x1 into y1 and x2 into y2, then 3 x1 plus 2 x2 must produce 3 y1 plus 2 y2.
A short echo kernel is flipped and slid across a recorded clap to produce the echoed clap.
A single click sent into a reverb pedal produces the decaying tail that is stored as h[n].
6.correctAnswer: If a circuit turns x1 into y1 and x2 into y2, then 3 x1 plus 2 x2 must produce 3 y1 plus 2 y2.
6.explanation: Both additivity and homogeneity are required, which together are the superposition rule.

6.question: Which situation illustrates Time invariance?
options: A tone at 1 kHz leaves a filter louder and slightly delayed, as predicted by H at that frequency.
A fixed echo unit delays any clap by 50 milliseconds, whether the clap is at noon or later.
A short echo kernel is flipped and slid across a recorded clap to produce the echoed clap.
A single click sent into a reverb pedal produces the decaying tail that is stored as h[n].
6.correctAnswer: A fixed echo unit delays any clap by 50 milliseconds, whether the clap is at noon or later.
6.explanation: The system rule does not depend on the absolute clock time at which the input is applied.

7.question: Which situation illustrates Convolution?
options: A clarinet note is written as a fundamental plus weaker harmonics at integer multiples of that pitch.
A tone at 1 kHz leaves a filter louder and slightly delayed, as predicted by H at that frequency.
A short echo kernel is flipped and slid across a recorded clap to produce the echoed clap.
A single click sent into a reverb pedal produces the decaying tail that is stored as h[n].
7.correctAnswer: A short echo kernel is flipped and slid across a recorded clap to produce the echoed clap.
7.explanation: For a discrete LTI system the output sample is the sum over k of x[k] times h[n-k].

7.question: Which situation illustrates Impulse response?
options: A single click sent into a reverb pedal produces the decaying tail that is stored as h[n].
A single rectangular pulse, which does not repeat, has a sinc-shaped continuous spectrum.
A tone at 1 kHz leaves a filter louder and slightly delayed, as predicted by H at that frequency.
A clarinet note is written as a fundamental plus weaker harmonics at integer multiples of that pitch.
7.correctAnswer: A single click sent into a reverb pedal produces the decaying tail that is stored as h[n].
7.explanation: An LTI system is completely described by this response, because every input is a combination of impulses.

7.question: Which situation illustrates Frequency response?
options: A tone at 1 kHz leaves a filter louder and slightly delayed, as predicted by H at that frequency.
A clarinet note is written as a fundamental plus weaker harmonics at integer multiples of that pitch.
A single rectangular pulse, which does not repeat, has a sinc-shaped continuous spectrum.
A five-sample discrete pulse has a DTFT that is a smooth function of frequency and repeats every 2 pi.
7.correctAnswer: A tone at 1 kHz leaves a filter louder and slightly delayed, as predicted by H at that frequency.
7.explanation: Complex exponentials are eigenfunctions of LTI systems, and the eigenvalue at each frequency is this response.

7.question: Which situation illustrates Fourier series?
options: A five-sample discrete pulse has a DTFT that is a smooth function of frequency and repeats every 2 pi.
A single rectangular pulse, which does not repeat, has a sinc-shaped continuous spectrum.
A clarinet note is written as a fundamental plus weaker harmonics at integer multiples of that pitch.
The charging curve of a capacitor is transformed in s so a differential equation becomes algebra.
7.correctAnswer: A clarinet note is written as a fundamental plus weaker harmonics at integer multiples of that pitch.
7.explanation: A periodic signal repeats, so its spectrum sits on discrete harmonic frequencies of the fundamental.

7.question: Which situation illustrates Fourier transform?
options: The charging curve of a capacitor is transformed in s so a differential equation becomes algebra.
A single rectangular pulse, which does not repeat, has a sinc-shaped continuous spectrum.
A five-sample discrete pulse has a DTFT that is a smooth function of frequency and repeats every 2 pi.
A geometric sequence a to the n, for n at least 0, has a z-transform that is a simple rational function.
7.correctAnswer: A single rectangular pulse, which does not repeat, has a sinc-shaped continuous spectrum.
7.explanation: The continuous-time Fourier transform integrates x(t) against complex exponentials to obtain a frequency function X(jw).

7.question: Which situation illustrates Discrete-time Fourier transform?
options: A five-sample discrete pulse has a DTFT that is a smooth function of frequency and repeats every 2 pi.
The charging curve of a capacitor is transformed in s so a differential equation becomes algebra.
The transform 1 over (1 - 2 z inverse) can be a right-sided or left-sided sequence depending on the region.
A geometric sequence a to the n, for n at least 0, has a z-transform that is a simple rational function.
7.correctAnswer: A five-sample discrete pulse has a DTFT that is a smooth function of frequency and repeats every 2 pi.
7.explanation: The transform sums x[n] exp(-j w n), and the result repeats every 2 pi because n is an integer.

7.question: Which situation illustrates Laplace transform?
options: A geometric sequence a to the n, for n at least 0, has a z-transform that is a simple rational function.
The transform 1 over (1 - 2 z inverse) can be a right-sided or left-sided sequence depending on the region.
The charging curve of a capacitor is transformed in s so a differential equation becomes algebra.
A resting RC filter has H(s) equal to 1 over (1 plus R C s).
7.correctAnswer: The charging curve of a capacitor is transformed in s so a differential equation becomes algebra.
7.explanation: The factor exp(-s t) lets the transform converge for unstable or growing signals inside a region of convergence and exposes poles.

7.question: Which situation illustrates Z-transform?
options: The transform 1 over (1 - 2 z inverse) can be a right-sided or left-sided sequence depending on the region.
A resting RC filter has H(s) equal to 1 over (1 plus R C s).
A geometric sequence a to the n, for n at least 0, has a z-transform that is a simple rational function.
A system H(s) = 1 over (s plus 2) has a single pole at s = -2.
7.correctAnswer: A geometric sequence a to the n, for n at least 0, has a z-transform that is a simple rational function.
7.explanation: Powers of z replace the continuous exponential, and the region of convergence decides which sequence the transform represents.

7.question: Which situation illustrates Region of convergence?
options: The transform 1 over (1 - 2 z inverse) can be a right-sided or left-sided sequence depending on the region.
H(z) = 1 minus z inverse has a zero at z = 1, so it rejects a constant input.
A resting RC filter has H(s) equal to 1 over (1 plus R C s).
A system H(s) = 1 over (s plus 2) has a single pole at s = -2.
7.correctAnswer: The transform 1 over (1 - 2 z inverse) can be a right-sided or left-sided sequence depending on the region.
7.explanation: Without the region, a rational transform can correspond to more than one time signal.

7.question: Which situation illustrates Transfer function?
options: A system H(s) = 1 over (s plus 2) has a single pole at s = -2.
A hi-fi rumble filter keeps bass and midrange but weakens a 20 kHz hiss.
H(z) = 1 minus z inverse has a zero at z = 1, so it rejects a constant input.
A resting RC filter has H(s) equal to 1 over (1 plus R C s).
7.correctAnswer: A resting RC filter has H(s) equal to 1 over (1 plus R C s).
7.explanation: With zero initial conditions, Y(s) equals H(s) times X(s), so H(s) is that ratio, and likewise for H(z).

8.question: Which situation illustrates Pole?
options: H(z) = 1 minus z inverse has a zero at z = 1, so it rejects a constant input.
A hi-fi rumble filter keeps bass and midrange but weakens a 20 kHz hiss.
A system H(s) = 1 over (s plus 2) has a single pole at s = -2.
An audio high-pass removes a 50 Hz hum while leaving a 2 kHz flute note intact.
8.correctAnswer: A system H(s) = 1 over (s plus 2) has a single pole at s = -2.
8.explanation: The denominator vanishes at a pole and the numerator does not, so the transfer function goes to infinity there.

8.question: Which situation illustrates Zero?
options: An audio high-pass removes a 50 Hz hum while leaving a 2 kHz flute note intact.
A hi-fi rumble filter keeps bass and midrange but weakens a 20 kHz hiss.
A radio tuner keeps a station around 98 MHz and rejects both lower and higher channels.
H(z) = 1 minus z inverse has a zero at z = 1, so it rejects a constant input.
8.correctAnswer: H(z) = 1 minus z inverse has a zero at z = 1, so it rejects a constant input.
8.explanation: The numerator is zero while the denominator is not, so the transfer function itself is zero at that point.

8.question: Which situation illustrates Low-pass filter?
options: A hi-fi rumble filter keeps bass and midrange but weakens a 20 kHz hiss.
A real-time speaker can react to a clap only after the clap, never before it happens.
A radio tuner keeps a station around 98 MHz and rejects both lower and higher channels.
An audio high-pass removes a 50 Hz hum while leaving a 2 kHz flute note intact.
8.correctAnswer: A hi-fi rumble filter keeps bass and midrange but weakens a 20 kHz hiss.
8.explanation: Its passband sits next to zero frequency and its stopband occupies the high frequencies.

8.question: Which situation illustrates High-pass filter?
options: A decaying exponential impulse response stays absolutely summable, so a bounded tone cannot make the output explode.
An audio high-pass removes a 50 Hz hum while leaving a 2 kHz flute note intact.
A radio tuner keeps a station around 98 MHz and rejects both lower and higher channels.
A real-time speaker can react to a clap only after the clap, never before it happens.
8.correctAnswer: An audio high-pass removes a 50 Hz hum while leaving a 2 kHz flute note intact.
8.explanation: The stopband includes zero frequency and the passband lies above the cutoff.

8.question: Which situation illustrates Band-pass filter?
options: A real-time speaker can react to a clap only after the clap, never before it happens.
A decaying exponential impulse response stays absolutely summable, so a bounded tone cannot make the output explode.
A radio tuner keeps a station around 98 MHz and rejects both lower and higher channels.
A test sequence contains a 1 at n = 0 and zeros at all other stored indexes.
8.correctAnswer: A radio tuner keeps a station around 98 MHz and rejects both lower and higher channels.
8.explanation: Two cutoffs bound a single passband that does not include zero frequency or the extreme highs.

8.question: Which situation illustrates Causality?
options: A switch applies 1 volt at t = 0 and holds that voltage for all later time.
A decaying exponential impulse response stays absolutely summable, so a bounded tone cannot make the output explode.
A test sequence contains a 1 at n = 0 and zeros at all other stored indexes.
A real-time speaker can react to a clap only after the clap, never before it happens.
8.correctAnswer: A real-time speaker can react to a clap only after the clap, never before it happens.
8.explanation: For an LTI system this is equivalent to the impulse response being zero before time zero.

8.question: Which situation illustrates BIBO stability?
options: A decaying exponential impulse response stays absolutely summable, so a bounded tone cannot make the output explode.
A switch applies 1 volt at t = 0 and holds that voltage for all later time.
A cosine wave has the same voltage at time -t as at time t.
A test sequence contains a 1 at n = 0 and zeros at all other stored indexes.
8.correctAnswer: A decaying exponential impulse response stays absolutely summable, so a bounded tone cannot make the output explode.
8.explanation: An LTI system is BIBO stable exactly when its impulse response is absolutely integrable or absolutely summable.

8.question: Which situation illustrates Unit impulse?
options: A cosine wave has the same voltage at time -t as at time t.
A test sequence contains a 1 at n = 0 and zeros at all other stored indexes.
A switch applies 1 volt at t = 0 and holds that voltage for all later time.
A sine wave at time -t is the negative of the sine wave at time t.
8.correctAnswer: A test sequence contains a 1 at n = 0 and zeros at all other stored indexes.
8.explanation: That single 1 at the origin is the discrete unit sample used to probe an LTI system.

8.question: Which situation illustrates Unit step?
options: A cosine wave has the same voltage at time -t as at time t.
A switch applies 1 volt at t = 0 and holds that voltage for all later time.
A sine wave at time -t is the negative of the sine wave at time t.
A clock square wave looks identical after every 1 millisecond shift.
8.correctAnswer: A switch applies 1 volt at t = 0 and holds that voltage for all later time.
8.explanation: The step turns on at the origin and stays on, which is the discrete or continuous unit step.

8.question: Which situation illustrates Even signal?
options: A cosine wave has the same voltage at time -t as at time t.
A clock square wave looks identical after every 1 millisecond shift.
A sine wave at time -t is the negative of the sine wave at time t.
A single finite-length beep has finite energy and then stays at zero.
8.correctAnswer: A cosine wave has the same voltage at time -t as at time t.
8.explanation: Symmetry about the origin means the waveform on the left is a mirror of the waveform on the right.

9.question: Which situation illustrates Odd signal?
options: A sine wave that has always been on and never ends has finite average power and infinite energy.
A clock square wave looks identical after every 1 millisecond shift.
A single finite-length beep has finite energy and then stays at zero.
A sine wave at time -t is the negative of the sine wave at time t.
9.correctAnswer: A sine wave at time -t is the negative of the sine wave at time t.
9.explanation: The left side is an upside-down copy of the right side, which forces the value at time zero to be 0 for an ordinary function.

9.question: Which situation illustrates Periodic signal?
options: A digital-to-analog pin holds 0.5 volts steady until the next code arrives and the level jumps.
A sine wave that has always been on and never ends has finite average power and infinite energy.
A clock square wave looks identical after every 1 millisecond shift.
A single finite-length beep has finite energy and then stays at zero.
9.correctAnswer: A clock square wave looks identical after every 1 millisecond shift.
9.explanation: There exists T greater than 0 such that shifting the signal by T leaves it unchanged.

9.question: Which situation illustrates Energy signal?
options: A sine wave that has always been on and never ends has finite average power and infinite energy.
A digital-to-analog pin holds 0.5 volts steady until the next code arrives and the level jumps.
At 1 kHz a filter leaves the tone amplitude unchanged but delays the peaks by a quarter cycle.
A single finite-length beep has finite energy and then stays at zero.
9.correctAnswer: A single finite-length beep has finite energy and then stays at zero.
9.explanation: Finite energy usually means the signal dies out, so its average power over infinite time is zero.

9.question: Which situation illustrates Power signal?
options: A sine wave that has always been on and never ends has finite average power and infinite energy.
A short radio burst centered at 10 kHz is delayed by 2 milliseconds, matching the local phase slope.
At 1 kHz a filter leaves the tone amplitude unchanged but delays the peaks by a quarter cycle.
A digital-to-analog pin holds 0.5 volts steady until the next code arrives and the level jumps.
9.correctAnswer: A sine wave that has always been on and never ends has finite average power and infinite energy.
9.explanation: Persistent signals such as everlasting sinusoids spread infinite energy over infinite time but keep a finite average power.

9.question: Which situation illustrates Zero-order hold?
options: A short radio burst centered at 10 kHz is delayed by 2 milliseconds, matching the local phase slope.
A digital-to-analog pin holds 0.5 volts steady until the next code arrives and the level jumps.
At 1 kHz a filter leaves the tone amplitude unchanged but delays the peaks by a quarter cycle.
A complex tone exp(j w t) enters a filter and leaves as H(jw) times the same tone.
9.correctAnswer: A digital-to-analog pin holds 0.5 volts steady until the next code arrives and the level jumps.
9.explanation: Between sampling instants the output is a flat step equal to the most recent sample.

9.question: Which situation illustrates Phase response?
options: At 1 kHz a filter leaves the tone amplitude unchanged but delays the peaks by a quarter cycle.
A complex tone exp(j w t) enters a filter and leaves as H(jw) times the same tone.
A short radio burst centered at 10 kHz is delayed by 2 milliseconds, matching the local phase slope.
The RC circuit law R C dy/dt plus y equals x relates capacitor voltage to the source.
9.correctAnswer: At 1 kHz a filter leaves the tone amplitude unchanged but delays the peaks by a quarter cycle.
9.explanation: The frequency response is complex, and its argument is the phase shift applied to a complex exponential.

9.question: Which situation illustrates Group delay?
options: A smoother sets y[n] equal to 0.5 y[n-1] plus 0.5 x[n].
A complex tone exp(j w t) enters a filter and leaves as H(jw) times the same tone.
A short radio burst centered at 10 kHz is delayed by 2 milliseconds, matching the local phase slope.
The RC circuit law R C dy/dt plus y equals x relates capacitor voltage to the source.
9.correctAnswer: A short radio burst centered at 10 kHz is delayed by 2 milliseconds, matching the local phase slope.
9.explanation: A narrowband packet is delayed by the negative derivative of phase, not merely by the phase divided by frequency.

9.question: Which situation illustrates Eigenfunction property?
options: A 1 kHz sine is multiplied by impulses spaced every 0.1 millisecond to form weighted spikes.
A complex tone exp(j w t) enters a filter and leaves as H(jw) times the same tone.
The RC circuit law R C dy/dt plus y equals x relates capacitor voltage to the source.
A smoother sets y[n] equal to 0.5 y[n-1] plus 0.5 x[n].
9.correctAnswer: A complex tone exp(j w t) enters a filter and leaves as H(jw) times the same tone.
9.explanation: Exponentials pass through LTI systems as the same exponential multiplied by H at that frequency.

9.question: Which situation illustrates Differential equation model?
options: Samples of a bandlimited tone are each replaced by a sinc and added to redraw the smooth tone.
A smoother sets y[n] equal to 0.5 y[n-1] plus 0.5 x[n].
A 1 kHz sine is multiplied by impulses spaced every 0.1 millisecond to form weighted spikes.
The RC circuit law R C dy/dt plus y equals x relates capacitor voltage to the source.
9.correctAnswer: The RC circuit law R C dy/dt plus y equals x relates capacitor voltage to the source.
9.explanation: Linear constant-coefficient differential equations are the continuous-time models whose transfer functions are rational in s.

9.question: Which situation illustrates Difference equation?
options: An RC low-pass is quoted with a cutoff of 1 kHz, near the half-power point of its curve.
A smoother sets y[n] equal to 0.5 y[n-1] plus 0.5 x[n].
A 1 kHz sine is multiplied by impulses spaced every 0.1 millisecond to form weighted spikes.
Samples of a bandlimited tone are each replaced by a sinc and added to redraw the smooth tone.
9.correctAnswer: A smoother sets y[n] equal to 0.5 y[n-1] plus 0.5 x[n].
9.explanation: Constant-coefficient difference equations are the discrete-time models with rational transfer functions in z.

10.question: Which situation illustrates Impulse-train sampling?
options: An RC low-pass is quoted with a cutoff of 1 kHz, near the half-power point of its curve.
Samples of a bandlimited tone are each replaced by a sinc and added to redraw the smooth tone.
A 1 kHz sine is multiplied by impulses spaced every 0.1 millisecond to form weighted spikes.
A speech low-pass treats 0 to 3.4 kHz as the band that should come through clearly.
10.correctAnswer: A 1 kHz sine is multiplied by impulses spaced every 0.1 millisecond to form weighted spikes.
10.explanation: Each impulse picks out the signal value at one sampling instant, which is the ideal model of uniform sampling.

10.question: Which situation illustrates Sinc interpolation?
options: A speech low-pass treats frequencies above 4.6 kHz as the band that should be heavily reduced.
A speech low-pass treats 0 to 3.4 kHz as the band that should come through clearly.
An RC low-pass is quoted with a cutoff of 1 kHz, near the half-power point of its curve.
Samples of a bandlimited tone are each replaced by a sinc and added to redraw the smooth tone.
10.correctAnswer: Samples of a bandlimited tone are each replaced by a sinc and added to redraw the smooth tone.
10.explanation: When the sampling theorem holds, the sinc sum equals the original bandlimited continuous signal.

10.question: Which situation illustrates Cutoff frequency?
options: A speech low-pass treats 0 to 3.4 kHz as the band that should come through clearly.
Multiplying a speech spectrum by a low-pass H is equivalent to convolving the speech with h(t).
An RC low-pass is quoted with a cutoff of 1 kHz, near the half-power point of its curve.
A speech low-pass treats frequencies above 4.6 kHz as the band that should be heavily reduced.
10.correctAnswer: An RC low-pass is quoted with a cutoff of 1 kHz, near the half-power point of its curve.
10.explanation: The cutoff marks the boundary between the frequencies the filter is intended to pass and those it starts to reject.

10.question: Which situation illustrates Passband?
options: A speech low-pass treats frequencies above 4.6 kHz as the band that should be heavily reduced.
A speech low-pass treats 0 to 3.4 kHz as the band that should come through clearly.
Multiplying a speech spectrum by a low-pass H is equivalent to convolving the speech with h(t).
A resistor sets voltage equal to resistance times the current at the same instant.
10.correctAnswer: A speech low-pass treats 0 to 3.4 kHz as the band that should come through clearly.
10.explanation: Inside the passband the magnitude response stays close to the desired gain.

10.question: Which situation illustrates Stopband?
options: A sequence equal to one-half raised to n, for every n at least 0, has absolute values that sum to 2.
Multiplying a speech spectrum by a low-pass H is equivalent to convolving the speech with h(t).
A speech low-pass treats frequencies above 4.6 kHz as the band that should be heavily reduced.
A resistor sets voltage equal to resistance times the current at the same instant.
10.correctAnswer: A speech low-pass treats frequencies above 4.6 kHz as the band that should be heavily reduced.
10.explanation: Inside the stopband the magnitude response is kept below a required attenuation.

10.question: Which situation illustrates Convolution theorem?
options: A sequence equal to one-half raised to n, for every n at least 0, has absolute values that sum to 2.
A causal exponential is zero for negative time and nonzero afterward, so it is right-sided.
Multiplying a speech spectrum by a low-pass H is equivalent to convolving the speech with h(t).
A resistor sets voltage equal to resistance times the current at the same instant.
10.correctAnswer: Multiplying a speech spectrum by a low-pass H is equivalent to convolving the speech with h(t).
10.explanation: Filtering an input is convolution with h in time and multiplication by H in frequency.

10.question: Which situation illustrates Memoryless system?
options: A capacitor voltage already at 2 volts at t = 0 is handled with the one-sided Laplace transform.
A resistor sets voltage equal to resistance times the current at the same instant.
A sequence equal to one-half raised to n, for every n at least 0, has absolute values that sum to 2.
A causal exponential is zero for negative time and nonzero afterward, so it is right-sided.
10.correctAnswer: A resistor sets voltage equal to resistance times the current at the same instant.
10.explanation: No stored energy or past sample is required, so a resistor obeying Ohm's law is memoryless while a capacitor is not.

10.question: Which situation illustrates Absolute summability?
options: A sequence equal to one-half raised to n, for every n at least 0, has absolute values that sum to 2.
A microphone voltage recorded as a smooth waveform x(t) before any sampler runs.
A causal exponential is zero for negative time and nonzero afterward, so it is right-sided.
A capacitor voltage already at 2 volts at t = 0 is handled with the one-sided Laplace transform.
10.correctAnswer: A sequence equal to one-half raised to n, for every n at least 0, has absolute values that sum to 2.
10.explanation: For a discrete-time LTI system, a finite sum of absolute impulse-response values is necessary and sufficient for BIBO stability.

10.question: Which situation illustrates Right-sided signal?
options: A causal exponential is zero for negative time and nonzero afterward, so it is right-sided.
A capacitor voltage already at 2 volts at t = 0 is handled with the one-sided Laplace transform.
Daily closing temperatures form a sequence x[n] with one sample per day.
A microphone voltage recorded as a smooth waveform x(t) before any sampler runs.
10.correctAnswer: A causal exponential is zero for negative time and nonzero afterward, so it is right-sided.
10.explanation: Its nonzero part lies at and to the right of a start time on the time axis.

10.question: Which situation illustrates Unilateral Laplace transform?
options: A capacitor voltage already at 2 volts at t = 0 is handled with the one-sided Laplace transform.
Daily closing temperatures form a sequence x[n] with one sample per day.
An audio interface reads a microphone voltage 44100 times each second.
A microphone voltage recorded as a smooth waveform x(t) before any sampler runs.
10.correctAnswer: A capacitor voltage already at 2 volts at t = 0 is handled with the one-sided Laplace transform.
10.explanation: Starting the integral at the time origin lets initial conditions enter when derivatives are transformed.

11.question: An oscilloscope trace has a voltage at every real instant, not only at integer ticks. Which signal class is displayed?
options: A data partition
A continuous-time signal
A discrete-time sequence
A histogram
11.explanation: A value at every real time is a continuous-time signal.

11.question: A processor stores one temperature per integer hour and has no values between hours. Which signal class is stored?
options: An impulse train
A discrete-time signal
A continuous-time waveform
A phase curve
11.explanation: A sequence indexed by integers is a discrete-time signal.

11.question: An engineer measures a sensor voltage every 1 millisecond and stores only those readings. Which operation is that?
options: Zero-order hold
A linearity check
A Fourier integral
Sampling
11.explanation: Taking evenly spaced readings of a continuous waveform is sampling.

11.question: A signal contains nothing above 5 kHz. Which sampling rate is exactly the Nyquist rate for it?
options: 2.5 kHz
5 kHz
15 kHz
10 kHz
11.explanation: Twice the highest frequency, 2 times 5 kHz, is the Nyquist rate.

11.question: A converter samples at 8 kHz. Which frequency is its Nyquist frequency?
options: 4 kHz
16 kHz
2 kHz
8 kHz
11.explanation: Half of the 8 kHz sampling rate is 4 kHz.

11.question: A 9 kHz whistle sampled at 10 kHz is heard as 1 kHz. Which effect occurred?
options: Ideal reconstruction
Time invariance
A more stable pole
Aliasing
11.explanation: A high tone folding into a lower tone because sampling was too slow is aliasing.

11.question: A signal is bandlimited to 3 kHz and sampled at 8 kHz. Does the sampling theorem allow exact reconstruction?
options: No, because only periodic signals can be reconstructed
Yes, but only if the rate is exactly 3 kHz
Yes, because 8 kHz exceeds 6 kHz
No, because the rate must be below 3 kHz
11.explanation: The sampling rate is higher than twice the highest frequency, so the theorem says reconstruction is possible.

11.question: A filter obeys superposition, and delaying its input only delays its output by the same amount. Which model applies?
options: An LTI system
A time-varying gain
A decimator by ten
An adder with a constant offset
11.explanation: Linearity plus time invariance is exactly the LTI model used in Signal and Systems.

11.question: Doubling an audio input doubles the output, and the response to a sum is the sum of responses. Which property holds?
options: Instability
Time invariance alone
Linearity
Memorylessness
11.explanation: Scaling and adding inputs scales and adds outputs, which is linearity.

11.question: A processor behaves the same at every hour: delaying the input by 4 samples delays the output by 4 samples. Which property is that?
options: Causality
Finite energy
Linearity
Time invariance
11.explanation: A pure delay of the output when the input is delayed is time invariance.

12.question: Students compute each output sample as the sum over k of x[k] times h[n-k]. Which operation is that?
options: Zeroing negative time
Pointwise multiplication of transforms only
Convolution
Nyquist sampling
12.explanation: That sum is the convolution of the input with the impulse response.

12.question: A lab applies a unit sample at n = 0 and records the output sequence. What has been measured?
options: The frequency response at one tone
The stopband
The pole list
The impulse response
12.explanation: The output caused by a unit impulse is the impulse response.

12.question: A lab sweeps a sine wave and records the output amplitude and phase at each frequency. Which function is being measured?
options: The region of convergence
The frequency response
The input power
The impulse response
12.explanation: Gain and phase versus frequency form the frequency response.

12.question: A square wave repeats every 2 milliseconds and is expanded into a fundamental and its harmonics. Which representation is that?
options: A z-transform
A differential equation
A Fourier series
A continuous-time Fourier transform of a pulse
12.explanation: Harmonics of a periodic waveform are its Fourier series.

12.question: A non-repeating pulse is analyzed by integrating it against complex exponentials over all time. Which transform is that?
options: The continuous-time Fourier transform
A sampling-rate count
A z-transform
A Fourier series
12.explanation: The integral frequency analysis of an aperiodic continuous signal is the Fourier transform.

12.question: Students sum x[n] exp(-j w n) over n and obtain a spectrum that repeats every 2 pi. Which transform did they compute?
options: The continuous-time Fourier transform
The Laplace transform
The DTFT
A Fourier series
12.explanation: That sum, periodic in frequency with period 2 pi, is the discrete-time Fourier transform.

12.question: A continuous circuit equation is solved by transforming x(t) into a function of complex s. Which transform is used?
options: The Laplace transform
A Fourier series
The z-transform
Convolution
12.explanation: Continuous-time signals transformed in the complex variable s use the Laplace transform.

12.question: A discrete recurrence is solved by summing x[n] z to the -n. Which transform is that?
options: The z-transform
A moving average
A Fourier series
The Laplace transform
12.explanation: The power series in z of a discrete sequence is the z-transform.

12.question: Two different sequences share the same rational z-transform expression. What extra information separates them?
options: The passband
The region of convergence
The zeros
The support in time alone
12.explanation: The region of convergence selects which time signal a rational transform represents.

12.question: With zero initial conditions, the Laplace transform of the output divided by that of the input is formed. What is that ratio called?
options: The sampling period
The transfer function
The signal power
The impulse response sequence
12.explanation: The output-over-input transform of a resting LTI system is its transfer function.

13.question: H(s) blows up at s = -3 and the denominator is zero there. What is s = -3 called?
options: A step discontinuity
A pole
A zero
A passband edge
13.explanation: A denominator root where the transfer function is unbounded is a pole.

13.question: A filter's transfer function is exactly zero at z = -1, canceling a Nyquist-rate oscillation. What is z = -1 called?
options: A pole
The Nyquist frequency
The impulse start time
A zero
13.explanation: A numerator root that forces the transfer function to zero is a zero.

13.question: A designer wants to keep speech under 4 kHz and weaken everything above it. Which filter type is required?
options: A band-pass filter
A low-pass filter
An all-pass filter
A high-pass filter
13.explanation: Passing the low band and attenuating the high band is low-pass behavior.

13.question: A recording must lose a low rumble but keep bright cymbal frequencies. Which filter type fits?
options: A unit-step system
A band-pass filter
A low-pass filter
A high-pass filter
13.explanation: Attenuating lows and passing highs is high-pass behavior.

13.question: A receiver must keep 300 Hz to 3 kHz and reject both lower and higher frequencies. Which filter type is that?
options: A low-pass filter
A band-stop filter
A band-pass filter
A high-pass filter
13.explanation: A single middle passband bounded by two cutoffs is band-pass.

13.question: An LTI impulse response h[n] is zero for every negative n. Which property does that guarantee?
options: BIBO stability
Distortionless transmission
Causality
Use of future samples
13.explanation: An impulse response that is zero for negative time means the system is causal.

13.question: Every input that stays within a finite amplitude produces an output that also stays finite. Which property is that?
options: Causality
An all-pass response
BIBO stability
Memorylessness
13.explanation: Bounded inputs yielding bounded outputs is the definition of BIBO stability.

13.question: A test vector is 1 at n = 0 and 0 at every other n. Which standard signal is it?
options: The unit step
An impulse train
The unit impulse
A constant sequence
13.explanation: A lone 1 at index 0 is the discrete unit impulse.

13.question: A sequence is 0 for negative n and 1 for n = 0, 1, 2, and so on. Which standard signal is it?
options: A periodic signal
The unit impulse
The unit step
An odd signal
13.explanation: Turning on at time zero and staying at 1 is the unit step.

13.question: A waveform satisfies x(-t) = x(t) for every t. Which symmetry does it have?
options: Odd symmetry
Infinite energy
Even symmetry
Right-sided support
13.explanation: Equality with its time reverse is even symmetry.

14.question: A waveform satisfies x(-t) = -x(t) for every t. Which symmetry does it have?
options: Finite power
Even symmetry
Odd symmetry
Periodicity
14.explanation: A sign flip under time reversal is odd symmetry.

14.question: Shifting a waveform by 4 milliseconds leaves it identical, and 4 milliseconds is the smallest such shift. Which property is this?
options: Periodicity
Right-sidedness
Finite support
Finite energy
14.explanation: Exact repetition after a fixed interval means the signal is periodic.

14.question: A pulse is nonzero for only 20 milliseconds and its squared area is finite. Which energy-power class is it?
options: A constant everlasting sinusoid
A power signal
An energy signal
An everlasting square wave
14.explanation: Finite total squared magnitude means the pulse is an energy signal.

14.question: An everlasting cosine has a finite average of its squared value and infinite total energy. Which class is it?
options: The zero signal
A power signal
An energy signal
A signal undefined on the integers
14.explanation: Finite nonzero average power with infinite energy is a power signal.

14.question: Between samples a converter output stays flat at the last sample value. Which reconstructor is that?
options: Sinc interpolation
A future-sample polynomial
Sampling alone
A zero-order hold
14.explanation: Holding the latest sample constant until the next one is a zero-order hold.

14.question: A tone's amplitude is unchanged, but its peaks are shifted by a quarter cycle. Which part of the frequency response captures that shift?
options: The magnitude response
The impulse response
The pole list
The phase response
14.explanation: Phase shift versus frequency is the phase response.

14.question: Engineers estimate the delay of a narrowband pulse envelope from the slope of phase versus frequency. Which quantity is that?
options: The half-power cutoff
Phase at one frequency
Group delay
The sampling period
14.explanation: Envelope delay from the negative phase slope is group delay.

14.question: A complex exponential enters an LTI filter and exits as the same exponential times a complex constant. Which property explains that?
options: Convolution staying convolution in frequency
The eigenfunction property
Invariance of every waveform
Steps mapping to steps
14.explanation: Complex exponentials are eigenfunctions of LTI systems, scaled by the frequency response.

14.question: A circuit is described by R C dy/dt plus y equals the source voltage. Which model form is that?
options: A Fourier series
A difference equation
A memoryless map
A differential equation
14.explanation: A relation involving a continuous derivative of the output is a differential equation model.

14.question: A program computes each y[n] from y[n-1] and x[n] with fixed coefficients. Which equation type is that?
options: A difference equation
A Fourier integral
A differential equation
The sampling theorem
14.explanation: Relating discrete samples with fixed delays is a difference equation.

15.question: A textbook models sampling by multiplying x(t) by a periodic train of impulses. Which model is that?
options: Impulse-train sampling
Adding a step
Zero-order hold
Low-pass convolution
15.explanation: Multiplication by a periodic impulse train is the impulse-train sampling model.

15.question: Reconstruction sums shifted sinc pulses weighted by the samples of a properly sampled tone. Which method is that?
options: Zero-order hold
Amplitude quantization
Leaving spectral copies in place
Sinc interpolation
15.explanation: The ideal bandlimited reconstructor is a sum of sinc pulses.

15.question: A low-pass specification names 2 kHz as the edge where power gain is about half. Which specification number is that?
options: The sampling rate
The cutoff frequency
A far-away zero
The fundamental period
15.explanation: The half-power edge of the passband is a cutoff frequency.

15.question: A spec says frequencies from 0 to 1 kHz must be transmitted with almost no loss. What is that frequency interval called?
options: The causal support
The stopband
The passband
The unstable poles
15.explanation: The interval meant to pass with little loss is the passband.

15.question: A low-pass spec demands strong attenuation above 8 kHz. What is that high-frequency interval called?
options: The region of convergence
The passband
The stopband
The impulse support
15.explanation: The interval that must be strongly attenuated is the stopband.

15.question: An engineer multiplies a spectrum by H(jw) instead of convolving the waveform with h(t). Which theorem justifies that shortcut?
options: A claim that addition becomes multiplication
A claim that convolution stays convolution in frequency
The convolution theorem
A claim that sampling removes all frequencies
15.explanation: Time-domain convolution corresponds to multiplication of Fourier transforms.

15.question: An output sample y[n] equals 3 times x[n] and uses no other sample. Which system class is that?
options: A noncausal averager of future samples
A system with memory
A long convolution
Memoryless
15.explanation: Dependence on only the current input means the system is memoryless.

15.question: The absolute values of h[n] sum to a finite number. What does that imply for the discrete LTI system?
options: It must be unstable
It is BIBO stable
It must be periodic
It must be sampled too slowly
15.explanation: Absolute summability of h[n] is the BIBO stability test for discrete LTI systems.

15.question: A Laplace transform is known to come from a signal that is zero before t = 0. Which support class is that signal?
options: Periodic
Right-sided
Two-sided
Left-sided
15.explanation: Being zero before a finite start time makes the signal right-sided.

15.question: A circuit problem includes a nonzero capacitor voltage at t = 0 and ignores negative time. Which Laplace form fits?
options: A Fourier series
The unilateral Laplace transform
The bilateral Laplace transform
The z-transform
15.explanation: The integral from zero forward is the unilateral Laplace transform used with initial conditions.
